source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) Incremental structure-mapping (I-SME)
finding: I-SME takes base and target facts one at a time, keeps up to n best global mappings, and EXTENDs them with new kernels. A separate REMAP step clears the mappings and rebuilds from all kernels. Given all facts at once it gives the same result as SME.
numbers: Cost: match network is linear to quadratic in description size; greedy merge is linear in kernels. Matching stories of 67 and 52 expressions took 34 s on a 1994 PowerBook 165c.
limits: Incremental matching can be misled when only partial information is available, and early poor decisions mislead later steps. I-SME does not remap automatically: remap criteria are task-specific. It only reports what fraction of the possible structural score the current mappings hold. Hard filters; no human data of its own.
agent_relevance: S6 across rounds: keep the current mapping, extend it with new facts, and let code decide when to rebuild. Log the score fraction as the remap signal.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) I-SME simulation of Keane's serial attribute-mapping task
finding: Human order effect (Keane): when the singleton facts come last, people take about twice as long. I-SME, set to remap whenever an entity or attribute could not join the current mapping, did about twice as many remaps in that condition.
numbers: Human mean solve time (Keane, in press, second-hand): singleton-first 178.0 s, singleton-last 363.1 s. I-SME average remaps per example: 1.5 vs 3.0.
limits: The natural first guess TIMID=HUNGRY, TOM=FIDO cannot give a 1:1 mapping, so a late singleton forces a rebuild. Authors doubt the task tests analogy (no higher-order structure). Human numbers are second-hand; Keane's paper was not opened. The remap rule was chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: The order facts arrive in changes cost. If a fact that breaks the first guess comes late, expect rework. Present constraining facts first where we control order.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) MARS worked-example solver built on I-SME
finding: MARS solved a heater thermodynamics problem from a worked example by extending its mapping 5 times, each time taking equations from new candidate inferences. With the IDENTICAL-FUNCTIONS filter removed, it matched enthalpy h with temperature T and reached a simpler but wrong solution.
numbers: One worked problem (helium heater, answer 621.22 kW); 16-step solution; 5 mapping extensions. No accuracy statistics.
limits: One example, no human comparison, hand-built representations. Authors say correct filter use may come from expertise or metacognitive skill.
agent_relevance: Extending a mapping needs a guard against pairing quantities of different kinds. In S6, forbid a new correspondence between different relation types unless a check allows it.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) serial versus parallel argument; rivals IAM, ACME, LISA
finding: Authors propose parallel local matching and kernel building, then serial, capacity-limited merging. They argue IAM's fully serial design (each local match decided in order, backtracking to try alternatives) will not scale. Serial merging is offered as an account of 'More is Less' (Gentner & Ratterman 1991): extra shared structure speeds and improves mapping.
numbers: No new data. Rivals: IAM (Keane & Brayshaw 1988) serial throughout; ACME (Holyoak & Thagard 1989) parallel in concept; Hummel & Holyoak (1992) incremental scheme that cannot handle higher-order relations.
limits: Argument from plausibility. The experiment that would separate the accounts is not reported in this paper.
agent_relevance: Compare broadly at once, but commit to the merged mapping step by step. Do not decide each correspondence one at a time.

source: Keane (in press); Keane, Ledgeway, Duff (1994) Constraints on analogical mapping: a comparison of three models. Cognitive Science 18
finding: Founding human data on incremental mapping: giving the same attribute-mapping facts in a different serial order changes how long people take. Only second-hand numbers were seen, via the I-SME paper.
numbers: Second-hand: singleton-first 178.0 s vs singleton-last 363.1 s mean solve time. Subject count not seen.
limits: Publisher page returned HTTP 403; primary paper not opened. Subject N, errors and model fits unverified. Task is symbolic attribute mapping.
agent_relevance: Pointer only. Re-check numbers before citing in the schema.

source: Kotovsky & Gentner (1996) Comparison and categorization in the development of relational similarity (as described in Kandaswamy et al. 2014)
finding: Children can learn relational matches over a few trials when closely spaced, highly alignable pairs come first (progressive alignment). Age 4 was below chance on all but the easiest same-dimension, same-polarity triads; ages 6 and 8 saw the relational pattern better with first-order support.
numbers: Second-hand: 4-year-olds below chance except in the easiest condition; cross-dimension, opposite-polarity was hardest even at age 8. Exact cell percentages not read from the original.
limits: Original not opened. Child data.
agent_relevance: Order of examples matters: begin with the easy, highly alignable pair, then move to harder ones.

source: Kandaswamy, Forbus, Gentner (2014) Modeling learning via progressive alignment using interim generalizations
finding: A structure-mapping simulation builds an interim generalization from a close pair held in working memory, notices when re-representation is needed, and does it. It reproduces the easy-first learning pattern seen in children.
numbers: Model got 100% on same-dimension triads where children got 68% correct. Tables 1 to 4 give the cells. Model learned rapidly where children improved slowly.
limits: Model is more uniform and faster than children; stimuli are sketches encoded by CogSketch; one fixed encoding strategy.
agent_relevance: A running generalization (what stayed the same across rounds) can be the object S6 extends, rather than the raw last pair.

source: Lovett, Gentner, Forbus (2006) Simulating time-course phenomena in perceptual similarity via incremental encoding
finding: At very short limits people judge sameness mostly by attribute overlap; with more time relational structure takes over. The authors argue attributes are encoded before relations, so comparison runs on a partial, growing representation.
numbers: Goldstone & Medin (1994) deadlines 1 s, 1.84 s, 2.68 s: at 1 s cross-mapped matches (MOPs) and consistent matches (MIPs) raised false 'same' equally; at longer deadlines MOP influence dropped significantly. Sloutsky & Yarlas: base shown 2100 ms vs 150 ms.
limits: Simulation of two published studies, no new human data. The rival reading (attribute matches simply enter comparison first) is not fully ruled out.
agent_relevance: Early partial views favour surface overlap. Expect a first-round mapping to be surface-based and plan for relational repair.

source: Lovett, Gentner, Forbus, Sagi (2009) Using analogical mapping to simulate time-course phenomena in perceptual similarity. Cognitive Systems Research 10
finding: Journal version. Limited encoding time hurts detection of relation-only mismatches far more than attribute mismatches; comparison can run on incomplete representations; high-similarity pairs take longer to call different.
numbers: Gentner & Sagi shield study: 'different' responses 1380 ms for high-similarity pairs vs 880 ms for low-similarity pairs. Sloutsky & Yarlas encoding 150 ms vs 2100 ms.
limits: Visual same-different tasks, not verbal or problem-solving analogy. Fits are qualitative.
agent_relevance: A partial mapping is usable, but it carries a known surface bias that later rounds must correct.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. Nature Human Behaviour
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text analogy tasks with no training: digit matrices, letter strings, four-term verbal analogies, story analogies.
numbers: Digit matrices (human N=40): GPT-3 above human average, generative OR=1.88, p=0.005; multiple-choice OR=6.27, p=2.3e-8. Letter strings (human N=57): GPT-3 better on zero-generalization problems, OR=1.76, p=0.0007. Verbal analogies N=57; story analogies N=54.
limits: Whole problem given at once, so it does not test extending a mapping with later facts. Counterfactual critiques (next rows) challenge generality. GPT-3 text-davinci-003.
agent_relevance: Baseline: a model can form one mapping from a full description. Says nothing about revision.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: On letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets, human accuracy stayed high while GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 dropped sharply. A comprehension check showed the models mostly understood the permuted alphabets.
numbers: Prolific study: 136 recruited, some rejected; 14 problems each; 46 human samples per cell vs 57 in Webb et al. Webb used 100 generated problems per type. Humans above all GPT models on nearly every problem type.
limits: Humans scored higher than Webb's participants (different pool and protocol). Letter-string domain only; GPT-4 tested without code execution (see next row).
agent_relevance: Failures on rewired content mean brittle mappings. Test any mapping step on a mutated version of the problem (fits G3).

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Reply to Hodel & West and Lewis & Mitchell. GPT-4 with code execution solved counterfactual letter-string analogies at about human level; without it, performance matched the critics. The authors read the failure as a counting problem, not an analogy problem.
numbers: 46% (23/50) of GPT-4's errors used a valid alternative rule, vs 39% of errors in the human data of Lewis & Mitchell. Digit Matrices used counterfactual digit orderings in the original paper.
limits: The fix uses code execution, not a human-like route. Authors are the original claimants.
agent_relevance: Give the model a tool for index and counting work; some analogy failures are arithmetic failures. Code-checked tools fit the schema.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs: digit matrices
finding: On digit matrices, moving the blank position made GPT-4 fall to 0.480 from 0.813 on the original, while humans stayed roughly level across variants. Swapping digits for symbols changed little for humans or models.
numbers: Samples: humans 1,550 (Digits) and 1,000 each (Alt. Blank, Symbols); GPT models 2,916 / 1,466 / 2,100. GPT-4: Digits 0.813, Alt. Blank 0.480, Symbols 0.790.
limits: Text extraction of the table mixed row labels, so human and GPT-3.5 cells were not read reliably; only GPT-4's drop is used here.
agent_relevance: A layout change that leaves the logic intact can break a mapping. Re-map after reformatting.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs: story analogies
finding: On 18 far-analogy story problems, GPT-4 was biased by answer order and was hurt by paraphrasing the correct story. Humans showed no order bias. The correct story often shared sentence-level similarity with the source, a possible shortcut.
numbers: GPT-4 (Webb data) 0.89 (16/18) when the correct answer was first, 0.61 (11/18) when second. Their GPT-4 run: 0.86 (31/36) original vs 0.72 (26/36) paraphrased. Humans 0.78 (292/373) answer-first vs 0.78 (272/347) answer-second, 0.78 (564/720) overall.
limits: Only 18 stories; the paraphrase gap between GPT-4 and humans may not be significant (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Randomise the order in which candidates or facts are shown and compare outcomes across orders (G4: samples from one model are not independent).

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning. Journal of Memory and Language 145
finding: New tasks where words map to letter or symbol sequences, testing semantic structure and content. Strong models match humans in several conditions but differ on distractors and when the structure is enlarged.
numbers: GPT-4 mean match proportion about 0.7 in Categorial and Dual-attribute conditions (humans 0.7 and 0.4); in the remaining conditions GPT-4 falls to 0.2 to 0.3 and is significantly worse than humans in Numeric (coef -1.4781). Claude 3 matched humans in all conditions of one experiment.
limits: Models are distracted by random lexical items; GPT-4 and Llama-405B drop when 2x2 structure is enlarged, Claude 3 does not. Authors conclude LLMs are a how-possibly, not how-actually, account. One-shot, not incremental.
agent_relevance: Distractor words pull a mapping off course. Filter lexical distractors before new facts reach the mapping.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners. ICLR
finding: Prompting the model to recall related problems and solve them before the target beat 0-shot and 3-shot chain of thought across math and code, average gain about +4%.
numbers: GSM8K/MATH Acc@1 for GPT-3.5-turbo-16k: 3-shot CoT 11%, self-generated exemplars 13%, knowledge plus exemplars 15%; GPT-4 17% to 19% (table text interleaved, row assignment approximate).
limits: Single-pass analogy to self-made examples, not incremental mapping. Table extraction scrambled.
agent_relevance: Cheap prior: ask for analogous solved problems first. Weak evidence for mapping revision.

source: Khojasteh et al. (2026) YARN: enhancing structural mapping with LLM-derived abstractions for narrative analogy
finding: A pipeline splits stories into units, abstracts each unit, then scores a structural mapping. Mapping over raw event embeddings was below chance; with abstraction it beat prompt-only LLMs on harder far analogies.
numbers: StoryAnalogy-MCQ (360 items, 4 options, chance 0.25): Qwen3-8B mapping alone 0.17, with abstraction 0.46 vs best LLM-only 0.41; Llama-3.1-8B 0.45 vs 0.28 LLM-only. ARN (1,096 pairs, chance 0.50): Qwen far 0.47 vs zero-shot 0.52; near 0.69 vs CoT 0.79; Llama far 0.46 vs 0.42.
limits: 8B models only; ARN far results stay below the 50% random baseline in all settings; mapping is one-shot, not incremental.
agent_relevance: Abstract each fact before mapping. The mapping step needs a good representation more than a better matcher.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The curious case of analogies: investigating analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Inside LLMs, relational information is present in mid-upper layers when answers are right. Failures often lack relational information or fail to apply it to the new entity. Patching hidden states at key tokens rescued some failures.
numbers: Patching the first pair fixed up to 38.4% of incorrect cases (Gemma-7B); answer revision gains up to 38.1%. Gains in other models: Llama-2-13B +32.3%, Qwen2.5-14B +35.6% on the first measure.
limits: Open-weight models up to 14B; interpretability method, not a prompt; proportional and story analogies only.
agent_relevance: Failures are often at the apply step. After a mapping exists, force an explicit apply-to-target step and check it.

source: Opielka, Rosenbusch, Stevenson (2025) Analogical reasoning inside LLMs: concept vectors and the limits of abstraction
finding: Task vectors are not stable across format changes. A few attention heads hold stable concept vectors for verbal concepts like antonym, but abstract concepts like previous and next show order-based or format-based codes instead. A model can form a correct internal concept and still output a wrong answer.
numbers: Llama-3.1 70B, 600 in-context prompts. Previous/next: 98% on ordered-list items vs 62% on abstract previous/next.
limits: Open models; verbal concepts; internal-representation evidence, not behaviour.
agent_relevance: Abstract relations like next or before are a weak spot. Spell them out as explicit rules.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) I-RAVEN-X: generalization and robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs and reasoning models
finding: Reasoning models hold up better than plain LLMs on longer relation chains and wider ranges, but collapse under perceptual uncertainty.
numbers: Arithmetic accuracy: reasoning models 80.5% to 63.0%; plain LLMs 59.3% to 4.4%. Under uncertainty, task accuracy fell 61.8%; o3-mini to 17.0% and DeepSeek R1 to 22.8% vs 12.5% chance. Ten extra confounding attributes: o3-mini lost 11.2% task and 15.2% arithmetic accuracy.
limits: Symbolic I-RAVEN task; some text extraction unclear.
agent_relevance: Models cannot keep several probable mappings alive at once. Hold the set of candidate mappings in code.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation
finding: When a task arrives in pieces over turns (sharded), all 15 LLMs tested did much worse than with the full instruction. Models made early assumptions, proposed answers too soon and did not recover from a wrong turn. The closest LLM test of facts arriving over time.
numbers: Average drop 39% across six generation tasks; 200,000+ simulated conversations. Aptitude fell about 16%; unreliability rose 112%. Gap between best and worst run about 50 points per instruction. At temperature 0 for both sides, unreliability stayed about 30%.
limits: Tasks are code, database, math, actions and the like, not analogy. The user is an LLM simulator.
agent_relevance: Core S6 evidence: do not let the model carry a mapping built from early turns. Re-state all facts each round and rebuild.

source: Laban et al. (2025) lost in conversation: RECAP and SNOWBALL mitigation
finding: Repeating earlier facts helps but does not fix it. SNOWBALL (restate all previous shards every turn) recovered about 15-20% of the full-to-sharded loss with GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini.
numbers: Mitigation 15-20% of deterioration; still below FULL and CONCAT. RECAP (one final restatement) beat SNOWBALL but is unrealistic because the last turn is unknown in advance.
limits: Two models, four tasks. Authors argue for native multi-turn support in models.
agent_relevance: A program-run SNOWBALL (re-feed every fact each round) is a cheap but partial mitigation. Pair it with a rebuild when a check fails.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Premise order matters in reasoning with large language models
finding: Shuffling premise order in deductive problems cut accuracy by over 30% with the logic unchanged. Forward order (same as the proof) was best.
numbers: Drops up to 20 to 30% for GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L; for Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo from over 65% to below 25% (more than 40 points). R-GSM benchmark also shows a drop vs GSM8K.
limits: Deductive and math tasks, not analogy; 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Fact order changes the result. Run two or more orders of the facts and treat disagreement as a signal to rebuild.

source: Hodel & West (2023) counterfactual letter-string critique, as summarised in Webb et al. 2024 and Lewis & Mitchell 2024
finding: Argued that Webb's test problems resemble internet text. Only second-hand summaries read.
numbers: No numbers read from the original.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Contamination is a live rival explanation for apparent analogy success.

source: Burstein (1986); Falkenhainer (1987, 1990) PHINEAS; Keane & Brayshaw (1988) IAM, as cited in Forbus et al. 1994
finding: Lineage of incremental mapping: Burstein first modelled incremental analogical learning; PHINEAS ran a map and analyze cycle to discover physical theories; IAM was the first general incremental matcher and is serial throughout.
numbers: No numbers. Second-hand from the I-SME related-work text.
limits: Originals not opened.
agent_relevance: A map, analyze, remap cycle is the older template for a loop in S6.
